A count model that assumes the average and the spread of the counts are the same.
A count model for data more spread out than a Poisson allows. Used when a few sites carry many injuries.
A count model with two parts: whether a site can report any injury at all, and how many it then reports.
A way to score words by how often they appear here and how rare they are elsewhere. Used to match text.
A text ranking formula that scores documents against a query. A strong search baseline with no machine learning.
A sibling term under the same parent, such as two clauses in the same section. Easy for a system to confuse.
Tying an answer to the exact source passage it came from, so a reader can check it.
Finding the passages most likely to answer a question before anything is written.
A condition that makes error more or less likely, such as time pressure, poor labels, or fatigue.
A federal human-reliability framework built around how people take in and act on information.
A simple human-error method from the nuclear industry that adjusts a base error rate by a few conditions.
A human-error method that scores the working context first and predicts likely control of the task.
A classification of accident causes in four layers, from the act itself up to management decisions.
A broad mental task such as noticing, understanding, deciding, or acting. Errors are sorted by which one failed.
A written structure of terms and how they relate, so the same word means the same thing everywhere.
A mapping that says which term in one framework corresponds to which term in another.
A model that estimates relations among things you cannot measure directly, such as safety climate, from things you can.
Something you cannot measure directly, estimated from several questions or indicators that stand in for it.
A fit score for a model. Above about .95 means the model reproduces the data pattern well.
A fit score where lower is better. Below about .06 is usually treated as close fit.
How often a stated 95 percent interval really contains the true value when the method is repeated.
Resample your own data many times to see how much an estimate would move if the sample changed.
A third factor that drives both things you are comparing, and can fake a relation between them.
How well a score separates two groups. One is perfect, .5 is a coin flip.
How common the outcome is to begin with. A rare outcome makes most positive flags wrong.
Run the model thousands of times with random inputs to see the range of outcomes, not one number.
Your position in a ranked list. At the 76th percentile, 76 out of 100 peers are below you.
The set of sites you are compared against, chosen by industry code and size band.
